fact_label: Unsubsidized Affordable Care Act (ACA) marketplace premium (40yo)
notes: CITATION-INTEGRITY CHECK 2026-08-25 ([specialist], verification review): corrected a real comprehension error in the prior note. The unsubsidized sticker premium itself did NOT roughly double -- KFF's own reporting (independently confirmed via search) puts the 2025-to-2026 unsubsidized benchmark premium increase at ~18-26% nationally (the largest single-year jump in 8 years), and a specific 40-year-old benchmark figure moving ~$621 to ~$752/month over the same period -- consistent with, not double, the $687-750 range here. What genuinely 'more than doubled' (114%, KFF) is a DIFFERENT number: the average NET premium PAYMENT previously-subsidized enrollees now face out of pocket, since the enhanced subsidies that had been covering most of that gap expired Dec 31, 2025 ($888/year average net payment in 2025 -> $1,904/year in 2026) -- a real, distinct, and arguably more consequential finding for a subsidy-eligible enrollee than the sticker-price move alone, but it is not the same claim as 'the unsubsidized premium roughly doubled' and the two were incorrectly merged in the prior note. The KFF calculator URL itself is a dynamic tool (no static premium figures on the page to directly verify a $687-750 figure against) -- the range is independently plausible given the confirmed $621-752 spread across sources, but not confirmed to the dollar.

fact_label: Tennessee mid-decade congressional redistricting — a 50-year institutional norm reversed in 6 days
value_raw: Since 1972, Tennessee law barred the legislature from redrawing congressional districts between decennial apportionments. Following SCOTUS's April 29, 2026 ruling in Louisiana v. Callais, Gov. Bill Lee called a special session May 1, 2026; the 1972 bar was repealed and a new map (carving Memphis/Shelby County across three districts) both passed and were signed by May 7, 2026 — six calendar days
notes: Ballotpedia, Wikipedia, Tennessee Lookout. Tennessee NAACP sued challenging the new map; a three-judge state-court panel dismissed that specific challenge 2026-05-26 (tennesseelookout.com/2026/05/26), but separate federal-court challenges remain open as of — a live, only-partially-resolved legal fight, not settled the way Asheville's own Supreme Court contest is.

value_raw: Fall leaf season (esp. 2nd-3rd weeks of October) is the single busiest stretch of the year — Blue Ridge Parkway traffic backups on peak weekends, downtown parking/restaurant demand spikes, hotels and short-term rentals booked out months in advance at spiked rates; summer separately shows a documented 29.8% spike in visitor volume over baseline. Buncombe County drew ~14 million visitors in 2023 (most recent full-year figure), including 5 million overnight guests, generating $2.97 billion in visitor spending.
notes: Corroborated across uncorkedasheville.com, windowsoverwaterfalls.com (crowding pattern) and Explore Asheville/Asheville.com (visitor-volume and spending figures, 2023/2025). Crowding is sharply seasonal and geographically concentrated (downtown, Blue Ridge Parkway, River Arts District), not a constant year-round texture — a real, if smaller, positive-lever counterweight worth naming alongside the busy-season finding.

fact_label: Internet speed — advertised top-tier vs. measured city average
value_raw: AT&T Fiber reaches an estimated 49.6%-66.2% of the city at up to 5 Gbps symmetrical; Spectrum cable covers ~91% of the city at up to 2 Gbps download from ~$30/month. But one aggregator's own city-wide average download speed figure is just 30 Mbps — a fraction of what top-tier plans advertise.
notes: broadbandnow.com, cablepapa.com. Genuinely fast fiber/cable IS available to a majority of the city, and the average experienced speed is a fraction of that — the two figures are different kinds of evidence, not one confirming the other; same shape as Rincón's coverage-percentage-vs-lived-experience gap.

fact_label: Tourist-season crowding — summer peak, fall festival growth
value_raw: Summer carries ~34% of annual visitors and spring ~33%, with June/July/March running about twice as busy as the quietest winter months — a genuine winter off-season, unlike Asheville. Fall has grown sharply as its own draw: Hamilton County's visitor economy hit a record $1.8 billion in 2024 (+4% over 2023's ~$1.7B), with downtown bracing for 'hundreds of thousands' of fall-2025 visitors anchored by the inaugural World of Bluegrass festival plus 150+ area fall festivals.
notes: championtraveler.com/USNews Travel for the seasonal-visitor-share pattern, Chattanooga Times Free Press (2025-08-18, 2025-08-29) for the fall-2025 festival/spending figures. Reads as more diffuse across the calendar and more event-driven than Asheville's sharper single leaf-season peak — a real but smaller-magnitude version of the same seasonal-swing question. Tourism supports 8,500 local jobs.

fact_label: EPB gigabit fiber coverage and measured statewide speed
value_raw: EPB (city-owned electric utility) has run citywide gigabit fiber since 2010, escalating to 10 Gig (2015), 25 Gig (2022, aimed at businesses/remote workers), and a new 5 Gig symmetrical tier (July 2026). Chattanooga-area fiber coverage runs ~93% per provider-coverage aggregators. Ookla's own measured data puts Tennessee's statewide average download speed at 308 Mbps / 95 Mbps upload — a real, state-level (not Chattanooga-specific) measured figure, distinct from EPB's advertised tier ceilings.
notes: EPB newsroom (advertised tiers), Allconnect/Ookla Speedtest.net (measured statewide average), ispreports.org (93% coverage estimate). One aggregator's claimed Chattanooga-specific '17,141 Mbps' average is almost certainly a data-processing artifact (likely averaging maximum plan tiers, not measured real-world speed) — flagged, not used.

fact_label: Seasonal population/crowding swing — winter surf season vs. summer-through-fall low season
value_raw: Winter swells (roughly December-April) draw surfers and spring-break crowds to the Domes/Tres Palmas breaks, with December-February bringing the biggest waves, peak whale-watching, and the year's highest accommodation demand. April-October is the genuine low season — long flat-surf spells, markedly fewer visitors, lower prices. This quiet/cheap/uncrowded window overlaps almost exactly with Atlantic hurricane season (June-November) and the power grid's most exposed months — Rincón is least crowded exactly when it is most exposed to storm/grid risk, and busiest with visitors during its calmest weather.
notes: thesurfatlas.com, casabonitarinconpr.com for the surf-season crowd pattern; cross-referenced against the already-sourced hurricane-season/grid-fragility finding (see US-rincon:chronic-power-grid-fragility) for the seasonal overlap. A resident's actual yearly rhythm is shaped by both curves at once, not just the climate-stability headline number.
